::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .060", "p = .194", "p = .060", "p = .060", "p = .194"), Sentence = c("Tests of interaction were not significant for sex (p = .060) or race and ethnicity (p = .194).", "Tests of interaction were not significant for sex (p = .060) or race and ethnicity (p = .194).", "The test for a sex difference was not statistically significant (p = .060).", "Interaction tests: sex, p = .060; race and ethnicity, p = .194.", "Interaction tests: sex, p = .060; race and ethnicity, p = .194." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Despite established appetite-stimulating effects of cannabis use, binge eating is seldom assessed in these samples.
Its prevalence, clinical importance, and demographic reach among people with cannabis-involved drug use disorder are largely unknown.
We analyzed 12,591 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys who completed the eating disorder and substance use modules.

Using design-weighted estimation, we estimated prevalence of binge eating among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder and examined whether binge eating marks greater burden and disability and whether it differs by demographic group.
Recurrent binge eating affected 11.2% of adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder (95% CI [8.4, 14.7]).
Separately, 5.5% met criteria for DSM-IV binge eating disorder.
Prevalence rose across levels of cannabis involvement (adjusted OR per level = 2.11, 95% CI [1.75, 2.55]).
Adults with both conditions had the highest prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, major depression, and generalized anxiety disorder.
At least one lifetime suicide attempt was reported by 27.8% of this group and by only 3.3% of adults with neither condition.

Binge eating alone was associated with a level of functional disability comparable to cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone, while adults with both conditions had the highest WHODAS time out of role and role impairment scores.
Among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, binge eating also marked a more damaging drug course.
Among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder, recurrent binge eating was more prevalent among women (17.4%) than men (8.6%).
Men nevertheless made up an estimated 54.1% of affected adults.
Prevalence ranged from 9.7% to 12.3% across racial and ethnic groups.
Findings indicate that binge eating is common and linked with adverse outcomes among those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, thus warranting targeted interventions.
Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is a common and largely untreated condition in the United States.
In a national survey conducted in 2012 and 2013, 6.3% of adults met lifetime criteria for DSM-5 CUD and 2.5% met criteria in the past year (Hasin et al., 2016).

text.text: These studies began with young adults or with people seeking treatment for binge eating.
To our knowledge, none has estimated the prevalence of binge eating among adults with CUD in a nationally representative sample.
It also remains unclear whether binge eating marks a more severe clinical presentation among people with CUD.
Diagnostic definitions add further complication to this already limited literature.
BN is a diagnostic rule-out for BED (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
text.formatted: BN is a diagnostic rule-out for BED <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Analyses restricted to BED therefore exclude people who binge and also purge.
They also exclude people who report recurrent yet sub-clinical binge eating without meeting full criteria for any eating disorder.
Binge eating must therefore be examined along a graded continuum ranging from a behavioral phenotype (binge episodes at least twice weekly for at least three months) through DSM-IV BED and BN.
Whether binge eating deserves attention in CUD treatment also depends on who is affected.
Eating disorder research has historically centered young, White women from relatively affluent backgrounds (Alegria et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Eating disorder research has historically centered young, White women from relatively affluent backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alegria et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Based on these samples, there is no solid grounding for generalization of binge eating relevance to the more diverse populations typically included in substance use treatment and research.
However, findings from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys (CPES) argue for generalization in part.
For example, BED prevalence was similar across ethnic groups, and any binge eating was more common in ethnic minority groups than among non-Latino White adults (Marques et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, BED prevalence was similar across ethnic groups, and any binge eating was more common in ethnic minority groups than among non-Latino White adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Marques et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Whether the same holds among adults with CUD is unknown.

We leveraged the CPES, which pools three nationally representative surveys of U.S. adults that share a common diagnostic interview (Heeringa et al., 2004; Kessler & Üstün, 2004; Pennell et al., 2004), to examine prevalence and correlates of CUD co-occurring with binge eating across the diagnostic spectrum.

text.text: We had three aims: First, we estimated the prevalence of binge eating among adults with a CUD and tested whether binge eating prevalence increases with level of cannabis involvement.
Second, we compared adults with both conditions, either condition alone, or neither condition on psychiatric burden, drug use course, and functional impairment.
Third, we tested whether prevalence and the association between CUD and binge eating differ by sex, race, and ethnicity.

The Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys (CPES) pooled three nationally representative surveys of U.S. adults conducted between 2001 and 2003: the National Comorbidity Survey Replication (NCS-R), the National Survey of American Life, and the National Latino and Asian American Study (Heeringa et al., 2004).

text.text: Public-use data were obtained from the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (study 20240).

Because CPES codes diagnostic variables as not endorsed when respondents were not administered a given module, we restricted analyses to the 12,591 respondents who were administered both the eating disorder and substance use modules and had valid long-form sampling weights.

For analyses of psychiatric burden and functional disability, the analytic sample was classified into four mutually exclusive groups based on lifetime recurrent binge eating and cannabis-involved drug use disorder: neither condition (n = 11,219), binge eating only (n = 632), cannabis-involved drug use disorder only (n = 641), and both conditions (n = 99).

For prevalence analyses, adults were classified by level of cannabis involvement: no lifetime drug use (n = 7,728), cannabis use without a drug use disorder (n = 3,835), and cannabis-involved drug use disorder (n = 740).
Adults who used other drugs but did not have a cannabis-involved drug use disorder (n = 288) were retained in the sample and are reported in the supplementary materials.
Cannabis Involvement.
The CIDI screens individual drug classes separately but assesses DSM-IV drug abuse and dependence criteria across drugs in aggregate.

We defined three levels of cannabis involvement: no lifetime drug use, cannabis use without a drug use disorder, and cannabis-involved drug use disorder, defined as lifetime drug abuse or dependence among respondents with lifetime cannabis use (n = 740).
Among respondents in the cannabis-involved drug use disorder group, 128 reported cannabis as their only drug and therefore met criteria for a cannabis use disorder.
The remaining 612 also reported lifetime use of other drugs, so their drug use disorder could not be attributed specifically to cannabis.
Binge eating was examined along a graded continuum, consistent with prior analyses of these surveys (Hudson et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Binge eating was examined along a graded continuum, consistent with prior analyses of these surveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hudson et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Measures included recurrent binge eating, defined as eating binges at least twice weekly for several months based on the CIDI screening item; binge eating with loss of control; and DSM-IV binge eating disorder (BED) and bulimia nervosa (BN), based on CPES-supplied diagnostic algorithms.
BED was defined using the DSM-IV bulimia nervosa diagnostic hierarchy.
Measures referring to the past 12 months were used in sensitivity analyses.
In the NCS-R, the eating disorder module was administered to a random half of Part II respondents (Hudson et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In the NCS-R, the eating disorder module was administered to a random half of Part II respondents <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hudson et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Clinical Burden and Drug Use Course.

Clinical outcomes included lifetime suicidal ideation, suicide plans, and suicide attempts; lifetime major depression and generalized anxiety disorder; fair or poor self-rated mental and physical health; obesity, defined as a body mass index of 30 or higher; and current unemployment.
Drug use course indicators included giving up important activities because of drug use and continuing to use drugs despite physical or emotional problems.
Functional Disability.
Functional disability was assessed using World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) domain scores, which range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater disability.
We also examined the number of days in the past 30 days that health problems limited usual activities and self-rated performance on days worked during the past 30 days.

Self-rated work performance ranged from 0 to 10 and was administered only in the NCS-R. Days out of role were assessed in the NCS-R and NLAAS, and the WHODAS role impairment domain in the NCS-R and NSAL; the remaining WHODAS domains were assessed in all three surveys.
Covariates.
The primary pooled models included sex, age modeled with linear and quadratic terms, education, marital status, race and ethnicity, and source survey.

Demographicstratified gradient models used the same covariates except the stratifying variable and any covariate constant within that stratum: sex-stratified models retained race and ethnicity, and race-stratified models retained sex.
Both interaction models included the full covariate set.
All analyses accounted for the CPES survey design using stratum, cluster, and longform sampling weights with Taylor series linearization.
The analytic sample was treated as a subpopulation of the full survey sample.
Weighted prevalence estimates used logit-based 95% confidence intervals.
All adjusted models included the covariates listed above and accounted for the survey design.

Binary outcomes were analyzed using logistic regression and reported as odds ratios, continuous outcomes were analyzed using linear models and reported as adjusted mean differences, and count outcomes were analyzed using quasi-Poisson models and reported as rate ratios.
Analyses were conducted in R using the survey package (Lumley, 2004).

text.text: We estimated the weighted prevalence of each binge eating phenotype overall, at each level of cannabis involvement, and within the cannabis-involved drug use disorder group.
We tested the cannabis involvement gradient using logistic models with involvement level entered as an ordered variable, reporting the adjusted odds ratio for each one-level increase.
We also fit models using the full cannabis involvement group classification.
Additional analyses examined the reverse direction, with binge eating predicting cannabis outcomes, and described the order of onset among adults with both conditions.
Two sensitivity analyses were conducted.
First, gradient models were additionally adjusted for lifetime alcohol use disorder.
Second, we repeated analyses using binge eating measures referring to the past 12 months and cannabis use frequency during the past 12 months.
Psychiatric Burden and Drug Use Course.
We classified adults into four mutually exclusive groups: neither condition, binge eating only, cannabis-involved drug use disorder only, or both conditions.
We compared the weighted prevalence of nine psychiatric and functional outcomes across groups and estimated adjusted odds ratios using the neither-condition group as the reference.
Additive interaction was assessed using the relative excess risk due to interaction, with confidence intervals estimated using the delta method.
Within the cannabisinvolved drug use disorder group, we compared adults with and without recurrent binge eating on drug use course and treatment outcomes.
These analyses used logistic regression for binary outcomes and a quasi-Poisson model for years of drug problems.
Across the same four groups, we estimated weighted mean WHODAS domain scores and adjusted mean differences using the neither-condition group as the reference.
Days out of role were modeled using quasi-Poisson rate ratios.

To estimate the annual excess days out of role associated with co-occurring binge eating, we calculated the unadjusted difference in weighted 30-day means between adults with both conditions and those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder only, multiplied this difference by 12, and estimated a confidence interval using the delta method.
We also estimated adjusted differences in work performance among NCS-R respondents.
Within the cannabis-involved drug use disorder group, additional models estimated the association of recurrent binge eating with disability outcomes.
As a sensitivity analysis, disability models were additionally adjusted for lifetime major depression and generalized anxiety disorder.

Within the cannabis-involved drug use disorder group, we estimated the weighted prevalence of recurrent binge eating by sex and by race and ethnicity, as well as each demographic group's weighted share of all adults with recurrent binge eating.

We then estimated the cannabis involvement gradient separately within each demographic group and tested moderation using interaction terms between cannabis involvement level and sex and between cannabis involvement level and race and ethnicity.
Interaction terms were evaluated using design-adjusted Wald tests.

text.text: Recurrent binge eating affected 5.0% of the total sample (95% CI [4.4, 5.7]) and 3.1% of adults who reported no drug use (95% CI [2.6, 3.7]).
Prevalence increased to 6.9% among adults who used cannabis without a drug use disorder (95% CI [5.6, 8.5]) and was highest among adults with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder.

Within this group, prevalence was 11.2% overall (95% CI [8.4, 14.7]), 15.0% among those who reported cannabis as their only drug (95% CI [6.7, 30.3]), and 10.6% among those who also used other drugs (95% CI [7.9, 14.1]).
Within the cannabis-involved drug use disorder group, 5.5% met criteria for DSM-IV BED (95% CI [3.9, 7.8]) and 7.2% met criteria for BED or BN (95% CI [5.3, 9.8]).
In adjusted models, the odds of each binge eating phenotype approximately doubled with each increase in cannabis involvement level (adjusted ORs = 2.11 to 2.32, all p < .001).

text.text: Adults with both conditions had the highest prevalence of all suicidality outcomes and of mood and anxiety disorders.

A lifetime suicide attempt was reported by 27.8% of adults with both conditions, 17.3% of those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder only, 10.5% of those with binge eating only, and 3.3% of those with neither condition.
Compared with adults with neither condition, those with both conditions had substantially higher adjusted odds of a lifetime suicide attempt (adjusted OR = 7.94, 95% CI [3.85, 16.38]).

Adjusted odds were also elevated for suicidal ideation, suicide plans, major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and fair or poor mental and physical health (Table 2; full contrasts in Supplementary Table S5).

Other indicators of drug use course, treatment, and years of drug problems did not differ significantly (Supplementary Table S7 and Figure S4).

Role impairment showed the same pattern, with adjusted differences of 3.7, 3.1, and 9.4 points, respectively (all p < .05).

text.text: Recurrent binge eating was about twice as prevalent among women (17.4%, 95% CI [11.4, 25.6]) as among men (8.6%, 95% CI [5.5, 13.1]).
However, men accounted for 54.1% of adults with both conditions.
Prevalence did not differ significantly across racial and ethnic groups and ranged from 9.7% to 12.3%.
The cannabis involvement gradient was positive in every demographic subgroup, with adjusted ORs ranging from 1.58 to 2.49 (see Supplementary Figure S2).

Tests of interaction were not significant for sex (p = .060) or race and ethnicity (p = .194).
This study provides national estimates of binge eating co-occurrence among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder.
About one in nine of these adults reported recurrent binge eating and about one in eighteen met DSM-IV criteria for BED.

These rates are roughly two to four times those in the general population and among adults reporting no drug use (populationwide rates of recurrent binge eating and BED were 5.0% and 2.4%; rates among adults reporting no drug use were 3.1% and 1.3%).
Prevalence of binge eating also rose with level of cannabis involvement.
In terms of clinical burden, adults with both cannabis-involved drug use disorder and binge eating carried the highest prevalence of suicidality and of mood and anxiety disorders.
Binge eating alone was associated with disability comparable to that of a cannabisinvolved drug use disorder alone.
Adults with both conditions had the highest role impairment.
The added contribution of binge eating within the disorder group was directionally consistent but imprecise.
Restricting attention to BED would have understated the prevalence of recurrent binge eating among those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder by roughly half (5.5% versus 11.2%).
The overlap is also visible from the opposite direction. Wilkinson et al. (2024) found that more than 23% of treatment-seeking adults with binge eating reported recent cannabis use.

text.text: Recurrent binge eating was associated with higher odds of cannabis-involved drug use disorder.
The association was not an artifact of lifetime recall.
For example, past-year binge eating was more common among past-year cannabis users (5.1% and 4.8%) than among nonusers (1.9%).
Finally, among the 58 adults with both conditions and dateable onsets, binge eating preceded the first drug problem in 48% of cases and followed the first drug problem in 41% of cases.
This pattern is compatible with a bidirectional relationship.

At least one lifetime suicide attempt was reported by 27.8% of adults with both cannabisinvolved drug use disorder and binge eating, while prior suicide attempts were reported by only 17.3% of those with cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone, 10.5% with binge eating alone, and 3.3% with neither (i.e., those with both conditions had 7.94 times higher adjusted odds of suicide attempt than those with neither (95% CI [3.85, 16.38])).

Among those with cannabisinvolved drug use disorder, recurrent binge eating was also associated with having given up important activities because of drug use and with continued use despite physical or emotional problems.
Clinically, this suggests that binge eating identifies a subgroup of adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder who are at higher risk.
These adults may benefit from suicide risk assessment and from integrated treatment.
Future research should test in prospective cohorts whether binge eating predicts poorer response to cannabis treatment.
Trials should then evaluate whether adding binge eating treatment improves both cannabis and eating outcomes.
Replication in samples collected after DSM-5 and after cannabis legalization is also needed.
Binge eating is sometimes treated as a secondary concern in substance use research.
Our results do not support that view.
For example, binge eating alone was associated with a +11.5 point increase in time out of role.
The corresponding increase for cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone was +8.2 points.

These differences were not explained by co-occurring major depression or generalized anxiety disorder, indicating that binge eating confers disability beyond the internalizing conditions that commonly accompany it.

Adults with both conditions scored highest on role impairment (13.9 versus 8.2 among adults with binge eating alone, 7.0 among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone, and 4.5 among adults with neither condition).

They reported an average of 4.6 days out of role in the past 30 days versus 2.3 days among adults with neither condition (3.8 days among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder alone and 4.5 days among adults with binge eating alone).
The cost was not limited to missed days.
Adults with both conditions also performed worse on the days they did work, a pattern not seen with either condition alone.
Among adults with cannabis-involved drug use disorder, binge eating was associated with a directionally higher but imprecise adjusted difference in role impairment (+6.5 points).
The excess in role impairment exceeded the sum of the two single-condition excesses.
This pattern would indicate that the two conditions compound one another's impairment beyond a simple sum, although formal tests of additive interaction did not reach statistical significance.

Women with a cannabis-involved drug use disorder were about twice as likely as men to report recurrent binge eating (17.4% versus 8.6%), a difference that is consistent with the wider eating disorder literature (Hudson et al., 2007; Kessler et al., 2013).

text.text: In our data the cannabis gradient was positive in both sexes, though the association was stronger among women (adjusted OR = 2.44 versus 1.78 in men).
The test for a sex difference was not statistically significant (p = .060).

Prevalence of co-occurring cannabis-involved drug use disorder and binge eating did not differ significantly by race or ethnicity (9.7% to 12.3% across four groups), and the binge eating -cannabis involvement gradient was positive in every group (imprecise for Asian and other adults: adjusted OR = 1.58, 95% CI [0.93, 2.68]).
This agrees with evidence that BED prevalence is similar across ethnic groups in the CPES (Marques et al., 2011).

text.text: While a lack of significant differences is not proof of equivalence, there is no empirical basis for presuming binge eating to be irrelevant to racially minoritized patients with cannabis-involved drug use disorder.
Based on the above estimates in our sample, about one in nine adults with cannabisinvolved drug use disorder would screen positive for recurrent binge eating.
BED often goes undetected and untreated (Giel et al., 2022; Kessler et al., 2013).

text.text: Brief screening in substance use treatment settings, applied regardless of sex or race, is therefore well supported.
Psychosocial treatments can reduce cannabis use but enduring abstinence is uncommon (Connor et al., 2021).

text.text: Whether, and to what extent, untreated binge eating contributes to this outcome is a priority for future CUD treatment studies.
There are several limitations that must be considered when interpreting our results.
First, the design of CPES is cross-sectional and relies on retrospective reports from lay-administered interviews.

Second, the interview used assesses drug use disorder criteria in aggregate across drug classes, and a CUD-specific diagnosis was possible only for respondents who reported cannabis as their only drug (n = 128).
The remaining 612 of the 740 adults with a cannabisinvolved drug use disorder also met criteria involving other drugs.
The co-occurring group was small (n = 99) and some subgroup cells were modest (for example, 66 adults with the disorder in the Asian and other racial groups).
Interaction tests and within-group comparisons therefore had limited power.
Third, the CPES surveys were conducted between 2001 and 2003, predating DSM-5 diagnostic classification of BED and the later rise in CUD (Hasin et al., 2015).

DSM-IV criteria for BED require binge episodes at least twice weekly for six months.
The behavioral phenotype required episodes at least twice weekly for at least three months.
The diagnostic group is therefore nested within the phenotype group by design.
DSM-5 lowered the BED threshold to once weekly for three months (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

text.text: Because the CPES eating disorder module screened for binge eating at least twice weekly, respondents who met only the lower DSM-5 frequency threshold were not assessed further.
DSM-5 criteria therefore could not be applied retrospectively.
All prevalence estimates reported here are based on DSM-IV criteria and are likely conservative relative to estimates using current DSM-5 criteria.

Finally, the eating disorder module was administered to a random half of NCS-R Part II respondents, and the supplied CPES composite weights do not incorporate an adjustment for this module-level subsampling.
We therefore report weighted prevalences and associations rather than absolute national counts.
Binge eating is common, clinically important, and demographically widespread among U.S. adults with CUD.
Adults with both conditions carry a particularly high burden of suicidality and role impairment.
Cannabis research and treatment should assess binge eating routinely and across demographic groups.
